procedural_history.impugned_order: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be previous orders in Writ Petition (C) No. 473 of 2005, specifically the order dated 08.10.2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not applicable, as this is an original jurisdiction case in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court is currently reviewing a status report submitted in compliance with a previous order. The Court finds the report incomplete and directs that any future affidavits or status reports be shared with the Amicus Curiae in advance. The case is listed for further hearing in January 2019. The case was initiated *suo moto* (By Courts Motion).

directions: List the matter in the second week of January, 2019.

issue.issue_text: Status Report with regard to Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards

facts: The Supreme Court reviewed a status report concerning Child Welfare Committees (CWCs) and Juvenile Justice Boards (JJBs).
The Court found that the report was unclear and did not specify whether CWCs were in existence in all districts of the relevant states.
A counsel present in court acknowledged this deficiency.
The counsel committed to the Court that she would investigate the matter, take it up with the State Governments, and provide a complete status report.
law: The case operates under the legal framework of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) of Children Act, 2015, which governs the establishment and functioning of Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards.
application: The Court assessed the submitted status report against the requirement for clear and complete information on the establishment of CWCs.
Finding the report inadequate, the Court did not make a final ruling but instead addressed the lack of information.
The Court accepted the counsel's proposed course of action, which was to gather the missing information from the states and submit a new, complete report.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the status report was insufficient. It accepted the counsel's commitment to provide a complete report detailing the existence of Child Welfare Committees in all districts after taking the matter up with the respective State Governments.

arguments.issue_text: Status Report with regard to Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards
appellant_arguments: The learned Amicus Curiae and counsel for the NCPCR argued that the status reports submitted by the government were incomplete.
It was pointed out that some states had not yet provided information regarding the number of child care institutions registered under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015.
The Amicus Curiae stated that the advisory and information were provided on the day of the hearing, which was too late for a proper review.
respondent_arguments: The learned Additional Solicitor General (ASG) submitted a status report, implying compliance with the court's previous order.
The ASG informed the court that the suggestion to strengthen the National Institute for Public Cooperation and Child Development had been referred to the Department of Expenditure.

statutes.act_name: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) of Children Act, 2015

ratio_decidendi.ratio: State Governments have a judicially enforceable duty to ensure all child care institutions are registered under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) of Children Act, 2015, and to report this information to the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights.
obiter: Any affidavit or status report proposed to be filed should be handed over to the learned Amicus at least three days in advance.
When a draft policy is available, it should be circulated widely and given to the amicus curiae so that suggestions can be invited from all concerned.
The Ministry of Women and Child Development should take up the issue of incomplete reports with the States.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the status report submitted by the government was incomplete, as information for a large number of States/UTs was outdated. The court accepted the arguments of the Amicus Curiae and the NCPCR that reports were incomplete and that some states had failed to provide required information regarding the number of registered child care institutions. Furthermore, the court acknowledged that information was provided to the Amicus on the day of the hearing, which was insufficient time for a proper review, and directed that future filings must be provided at least three days in advance.
policy_considerations: The court emphasized that the required information and registration of child care institutions must be completed "at least for the sake of children who are living in the States concerned."

The court reiterated its previous direction that when a draft Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) is available, it should be circulated widely to invite suggestions from all concerned parties, promoting transparency and public participation.
